content: Mucopolysaccharidosis type VI (MPS VI), also known as Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome, is a rare genetic disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme arylsulfatase B. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of dermatan sulfate, which causes damage to lysosomes within cells. The clinical manifestations of MPS VI are primarily related to skeletal abnormalities, such as short stature and degenerative joint disease. Other symptoms include cardiac complications, reduced pulmonary function, eye-related issues, hepatosplenomegaly (enlarged liver and spleen), recurrent sinusitis and otitis, hearing loss, and sleep apnea. Importantly, intellectual function is typically unaffected. Symptoms usually become apparent by the age of two or three, although in some cases with slower progression, the disease may not present until adulthood. Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) using galsulfase, a recombinant form of human arylsulfatase B, has been proposed as a novel treatment for MPS VI. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of galsulfase ERT compared to other interventions, placebo, or no treatment. To gather evidence, electronic searches were conducted in various databases, including the Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, LILACS, the Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and ClinicalTrials.gov. The most recent searches were performed in June and August 2021. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled clinical trials comparing galsulfase ERT to other interventions or placebo. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, assessed the risk of bias, extracted data, and evaluated the certainty of the evidence using the GRADE criteria. Only one study met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 39 participants who were randomized to receive either galsulfase ERT or a placebo. The study was small and had an unclear risk of bias due to insufficient reporting on allocation generation and concealment methods. The evidence from this study was assessed as having very low certainty. After 24 weeks of treatment, it was uncertain whether there was a difference between the galsulfase and placebo groups in the 12-minute walk test, with a mean difference (MD) of 92.00 meters (95% confidence interval [CI]: 11.00 to 172.00). Similarly, for the three-minute stair climb, the MD was 5.70 (95% CI: -0.10 to 11.50), but the evidence was again of very low certainty. Regarding respiratory function, it was unclear whether galsulfase had any effect on forced vital capacity (FVC) in liters, as the evidence was insufficient. Cardiac function was not reported in the study. The study did find that galsulfase may reduce urinary glycosaminoglycan levels at 24 weeks, with an MD of -227.00 (95% CI: -264.00 to -190.00), based on low-certainty evidence. However, it was uncertain whether there were differences between the galsulfase and placebo groups in terms of adverse events, as the evidence was of very low certainty. The dose of galsulfase was generally well tolerated, with no significant differences in the frequency of drug-related adverse events, serious or severe adverse events, infusion-related reactions, or deaths between the two groups. Infusion-related reactions were more common in the galsulfase group but were managed by slowing the infusion rate or administering antihistamines or corticosteroids. No deaths occurred during the study. In conclusion, the findings of this review are based on a single small study with a 24-week randomized phase. The evidence is insufficient to determine whether galsulfase is more effective than placebo for improving outcomes such as the 12-minute walk test or the three-minute stair climb. Galsulfase may reduce urinary glycosaminoglycan levels, but its effects on cardiac and pulmonary function, liver and spleen volume, overnight apnea-hypopnea, height and weight, quality of life, and adverse events remain uncertain. Further research is needed to better understand the long-term effectiveness and safety of galsulfase ERT for MPS VI.
